# Vultr Joins the Agentic AI Foundation to Advance Open, Interoperable Agentic AI

5 min readOctober 22, 2026

Agentic AI is moving from experimentation to production. Agents need to reason, call tools, access data, interact with other agents, and operate across distributed environments. Making that work requires more than models. It requires infrastructure, orchestration, frameworks, and open protocols that work together. [...] It also reinforces the point that AI infrastructure cannot be reduced to GPUs. GPUs are critical for training and inference, but CPUs handle application logic, orchestration, data processing, networking, agent execution, and many of the services surrounding the model.

Production agentic AI needs the full stack.

## Building an open, composable AI stack [...] The goal is not for every organization to use the same stack. It is to let developers choose a model, run it on the compute that best fits the workload, orchestrate it with Kubernetes, connect it to tools and data, and build agents on top – without a single provider controlling every layer.

No single company will build that ecosystem alone.

title: Why AI Chips Made In The U.S. Are Being Sent To Taiwan — Creating A Major Bottleneck
body:
There's a new bottleneck in the AI chipmaking process that happens almost entirely in Asia right now: advanced packaging. It connects smaller chips together into a larger chip like a GPU, so it can communicate with data centers and more. As Nvidia books the majority of capacity, TSMC prepares to break ground on its first U.S. packaging plants, and Elon Musk taps Intel for ambitious custom chip plans in Texas. CNBC got an exclusive interview with TSMC and toured an Intel packaging plant in [...] [6:04] To understand why, let's break down the different types. Mini chips like CPUs, are mounted directly to the base substrate in what's known as 2D or flip chip packaging.
[6:14] But for more complex chips for AI like GPUs, chip makers need 2.5D packaging pioneered by TSMC
[6:21] in 2012 with what it calls CoWaS, chip on wafer on substrate, now used by customers like Nvidia, Google, Amazon and MediaTek.
[6:30] Chips are really side by side, so they're really 2D from that perspective. [...] [5:27] AI. Because as AI leaders like Nvidia progress their chip density and performance rapidly, their advanced packaging needs are evolving quickly, too.
[5:36] They want to put more and more GPUs, more and more high bandwidth memory into one package.
[5:42] And so we have shortages because this AI demand was a little bit unexpected.
[5:50] So people had not put in enough capacity.
[5:59] While packaging is a necessary step, the most advanced kind is what's in short supply.

title: A third of the global AI supply chain is ‘invisible’ to governments | University of Cambridge
body:
One Japanese firm has a 95% market share of a material needed for AI chips, the report shows. Even notorious chokepoints depend on other nations: the Dutch firm dominating EUV lithography (ASML) relies on essential parts controlled by German and US companies.

In fact, the study suggests that countries such as Japan, Germany, and some so-called middle powers – from Belgium to South Korea – have far more leverage over global AI production than even their own governments realise. [...] Another major “blind spot” is advanced packaging: connecting multiple semiconductor chips into high-performance AI processors essential for frontier models. This packaging is overwhelmingly concentrated in Asian countries and territories such as Taiwan, Vietnam and the Philippines.

“Policymakers focus on finished chips rather than the ecosystem behind them. They focus on GPUs but ignore the packaging operations needed to turn those chips into usable AI hardware,” said Liu. [...] The researchers point out that a Japanese company, Ajinomoto, controls more than 95% of the global supply of build-up film, an insulating material needed for advanced AI chip manufacturing.

“Japan’s strength comes from equipment, and without it there's no way you can produce the hardware,” said Liu. “The supply chain is sequential, so the trickle down could affect computing capacities of the top frontier models.”
